newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Asia helps CBOT agri trade to record, moans at cost.
newsitem.headline: Asia helps CBOT agri trade to record, moans at cost.

text.p: Asian interest in Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) overnight Project A trading has helped lift volume in agricultural products traded off the exchange floor to record levels, but problems remain, traders said on Thursday.
"The Project A system is very useful for our clients since its trading hours are the same as our working time," a grain trader at South Korea's Cheil Futures Inc said.

On Monday, some 3,794 agricultural contracts including wheat, corn, soybeans and soymeal were traded on Project A -- a record for the electronic trading system which began accepting agricultural orders in February.

"Our clients seem to use both sessions on the CBOT...they will enter a position during the Project A session and wind it up during the CBOT's day session and vice versa," the trader at Cheil said adding that his company's average trading volume on the system has now reached over 100 lots a month.
"The biggest monthly volume (on Project A) from a single client was recorded at 1,500 lots. It was a pure hedge against physical risks," said a trader with Korea Commodity Inc.

But South Korean traders said relatively low liquidity, low volume, the comparatively high spread between bid and ask quotes, and high charges on Project A compared with Chicago's open outcry trading session, all hinder the system's use.
These comments were echoed in Taiwan, another major East Asian importer of U.S. grains and oilseeds.
"Project A could not deal with all our orders in one tick (before prices move again), so CBOT day trade is still the only choice for us," said a buyer at Taiwan's Hui Shung Agriculture and Food Corp.
Taiwanese traders said domestic grain buyers usually purchase 54,000-tonne shipments, or about 400 futures lots, -- a size that is too large for Project A to process efficiently.

"We can always change our orders during CBOT day trade, which is hard to do on Project A," a buyer at the Members Feed Industry Group said. Other buyers said the system also adds significantly to costs over and above normal commissions.

"Project A would cost about US$3 per lot to trade, which could become significant for our large-sized shipments," a buyer at Taiwan's Breakfast Soybean Procurement Association said, adding that $3 a lot would add up to US$1,200 for a 54,000-tonne soybean shipment.
Most of Taiwan's major grain suppliers recommend that buyers do not use Project A and often refuse to take such orders.
"Our U.S. head office does not have the personnel to handle the night trade if buyers want to place orders," one said.
In Japan, arbitrage trading between Project A and Tokyo grain futures is becoming increasingly popular.
"Arbitrage between CBOT corn and Tokyo corn is (a) particularly attractive business. The two contracts are showing increasingly transparent price fluctuations," a Tokyo commodity broker said.
Trading volume in Tokyo corn futures during the first eight months of 1996 was 12.50 million lots, sharply up from 4.70 million lots during the same period of last year.
The strong rallies in world corn prices earlier this year helped push Japanese participants into the overnight CBOT system during the Asian trading day.
"Purchasing officials at local feed makers were carefully watching Project A trading in May and June," a senior Tokyo corn trader commented.
In Australia, where Sydney's markets are opening on the tail of Project A trading at 0330 GMT (1:30 p.m.), soybean and wheat are probably most actively traded on the system.
Project A is viewed as a direct conduit to the Chicago market, although not necessarily a precursor of things to come.

"We have noted that Project A bears almost no relationship to the (U.S.) night market," said Colin Lethbridge, of ANZ McCaughan Futures. "Project A can fall three to four cents and the U.S. will take it up 10, but you still use it as a tool."
It's not a huge market, but we've never had a problem getting a price if we're sort of in the money," Lethbridge said. "There's always someone on the other side."
There is also little arbitrage with the lightly-traded Sydney Futures Exchange wheat market, which has been running since late March.
Most traders agree that the main benefit of the system is the access it provides to the Chicago market.
"If you had a position and you wanted to get away, you've had time to see CBOT's close and digest it and time to see the local markets," another grains trader said.
"Yesterday, we were selling wheat at 4.35 (U.S. cents a bushel)... you couldn't get that on last night because Chicago opened up and just collapsed, but we got it on yesterday afternoon, " he said.
Because Project A opens most days on par with CBOT, it is viewed by the local traders as the first market where they can sell their book.

"If we are sitting down on the Sydney (futures Exchange) floor and buying and selling spreads between the months, we can offload our positions to the Chicago market and not wait until one-o'clock in the morning to do so," the trader added.
